title: Kedoshim: as yourself (Leviticus 19:18)
hook: "thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself"; Rabbi Akiva called it the great principle of the Torah

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, a verse that won't let anyone just watch. Your line was don't stand idly by. Today, two verses later, a line that has traveled far beyond the chapter.

This line turns up on posters, at weddings, in speeches, on bumper stickers. Words that familiar can slide right off. But it's only the second half of a verse. The first half rarely makes it onto the poster, and it changes how the famous part sounds. It's not about warm feelings for nice people. It's about the person who did harm last month, and the grudge that's been quietly kept ever since.
screen: `ON POSTERS AND BUMPER STICKERS.` → `THE HALF THAT COMES FIRST.` → `THE ONE WHO WRONGED YOU.`

segments.voice: The whole verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." The love comes right after the grudge. It's the alternative to revenge. The Jerusalem Talmud explains vengeance with a picture. Someone is cutting meat, the knife slips, and it cuts their hand. Would the cut hand turn around and stab the hand that held the knife? Of course not. They're one body. So, too, the people: hurting each other back is like a body attacking itself. Rabbi Akiva called this verse a great principle of the Torah, klal gadol. His colleague Ben Azzai named a different verse as greater still: the line in Genesis about the generations of Adam, the human being made in God's likeness. Love your neighbor might depend on how you feel about yourself, some explain; Ben Azzai's verse grounds it in every person's dignity. The two teachings sit side by side in the sources. And when a man asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel said: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn. As yourself: a measure every person carries.
screen: `NO VENGEANCE, NO GRUDGE.` · `ONE BODY: THE CUT HAND.` · `AKIVA: THE GREAT PRINCIPLE.` · `HILLEL ON ONE FOOT.` · then, large: `AS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of a neighbor, literal or not: the person next door, at the next desk, in the next seat, maybe even one you hold a small grudge against. Ask what you'd want if you were them today: a hand with groceries, a kind word, a returned favor, an apology accepted. Picture giving it.
Kedoshim. The portion with love thy neighbor as thyself, which Rabbi Akiva called the great principle of the Torah, set right after the ban on grudges.
Your line: as yourself. The love stands right where the grudge would be. Four hundred fourteen days now.

howItsDone: Some prayer books open the morning service with a line taking on the commandment of loving one's neighbor as oneself, a custom traced to the kabbalist Isaac Luria, and Hillel's summary is often taught in Jewish schools.

chat.meaning: The verse opens: don't take vengeance or bear a grudge, but love your neighbor as yourself. The love is the alternative to revenge.

Akiva.meaning: a great rabbi who called this verse the Torah's great principle

Ben Azzai.meaning: Akiva's colleague, who pointed to the verse about Adam

Hillel.meaning: a great sage who taught the whole Torah on one foot
